source_text: Ἆρον ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ, φησί, τὴν λύπην: καὶ γὰρ αὕτη ἀδελφή ἐστι τῆς διψυχίας καὶ τῆς ὀξυχολίας. Πῶς, φημί, κύριε, ἀδελφή ἐστι τούτων; ἄλλο γάρ μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ὀξυχολία καὶ ἄλλο διψυχία καὶ ἄλλο λύπη. Ἀσύνετος εἶ ἄνθρωπε, φησί, καὶ οὐ νοεῖς, ὅτι ἡ λύπη πάντων τῶν πνευμάτων πονηροτέρα ἐστὶ καὶ δεινοτάτη τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ παρὰ πάντα τὰ πνεύματα καταφθείρει τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ ἐκτρίβει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ πάλιν σώζει; Ἐγώ, φημί, κύριε, ἀσύνετός εἰμι καὶ οὐ συνίω τὰς παραβολὰς ταύτας. πῶς γὰρ δύναται ἐκτρίβειν καὶ πάλιν σώζειν, οὐ νοῶ. Ἄκουε, φησίν: οἱ μηδέποτε ἐρευνήσαντες περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας μηδὲ ἐπιζητήσαντες περὶ τῆς θεότητος, πιστεύσαντες δὲ μόνον, ἐμπεφυρμένοι δὲ πραγματείαις καὶ πλούτῳ καὶ φιλίαις ἐθνικαῖς καὶ ἄλλαις πολλαῖς πραγματείαις τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου: ὅσοι οὖν τούτοις πρόσκεινται, οὐ νοοῦσι τὰς παραβολὰς τῆς θεότητος: ἐπισκοτοῦνται γὰρ ὑπὸ τούτων τῶν πράξεων καὶ καταφθείρονται καὶ γίνονται κεχερσωμένοι. καθὼς οἱ ἀμπελῶνες οἱ καλοί, ὅταν ἀμελείας τύχωσι, χερσοῦνται ἀπὸ τῶν ἀκανθῶν καὶ βοτανῶν ποικίλων, οὕτως οἱ ἄνθρωποι οἱ πιστεύσαντες καὶ εἰς ταύτας τὰς πράξεις τὰς πολλὰς ἐμπίπτοντες τὰς προειρημένας, ἀποπλανῶνται ἀπὸ τῆς διανοίας αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως νοοῦσι περὶ δικαιοσύνης, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅταν ἀκούσωσι περὶ θεότητος καὶ ἀληθείας, ὁ νοῦς αὐτῶν περὶ τὴν πρᾶξιν αὐτῶν καταγίνεται, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως νοοῦσιν. οἱ δὲ φόβον ἔχοντες θεοῦ καὶ ἐρευνῶντες περὶ θεότητος καὶ ἀληθείας καὶ τὴν καρδίαν ἔχοντες πρὸς τὸν κύριον, πάντα τὰ λεγόμενα αὐτοῖς τάχιον νοοῦσι καὶ συνίουσιν, ὅτι ἔχουσι τὸν φόβον τοῦ κυρίου ἐν ἑαυτοῖς: ὅπου γὰρ ὁ κύριος κατοικεῖ, ἐκεῖ καὶ σύνεσις πολλή. κολλήθητι οὖν τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ πάντα συνήσεις καὶ νοήσεις. Ἄκουε οὖν, φησίν, ἀνόητε, πῶς ἡ λύπη ἐκτρίβει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ πάλιν σώζει: ὅταν ὁ δίψυχος ἐπιβάληται πρᾶξίν τινα καὶ ταύτης ἀποτύχῃ διὰ τὴν διψυχίαν αὐτοῦ, ἡ λύπη αὕτη εἰσπορεύεται εἰς τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον καὶ ἐκτρίβει αὐτό. εἶτα πάλιν ἡ ὀξυχολία ὅταν κολληθῇ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ περὶ πράγματός τινος, καὶ λίαν πικρανθῇ, πάλιν ἡ λύπη εἰσπορεύεται εἰς τὴν καρδίαν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦ ὀξυχολήσαντος, καὶ λυπεῖται ἐπὶ τῇ πράξει αὐτοῦ ᾗ ἔπραξε καὶ μετανοεῖ, ὅτι πονηρὸν εἰργάσατο. αὕτη οὖν ἡ λύπη δοκεῖ σωτηρίαν ἔχειν, ὅτι τὸ πονηρὸν πράξας μετενόησεν. ἀμφότεραι οὖν αἱ πράξεις λυποῦσι τὸ πνεῦμα: ἡ μὲν διψυχία, ὅτι οὐκ ἐπέτυχε τῆς πράξεως αὐτῆς, ἡ δὲ ὀξυχολία λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα, ὅτι ἔπραξε τὸ πονηρόν. ἀμφότερα οὖν λυπηρά ἐστι τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ, ἡ διψυχία καὶ ἡ ὀξυχολία. ἆρον οὖν ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ τὴν λύπην καὶ μὴ θλῖβε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ ἐν σοὶ κατοικοῦν, μήποτε ἐντεύξηται τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἀποστῇ ἀπὸ σοῦ. τὸ γὰρ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ δοθὲν εἰς τὴν σάρκα ταύτην λύπην οὐχ ὑποφέρει οὐδὲ στενοχωρίαν. Ἔνδυσαι οὖν τὴν ἱλαρότητα, τὴν πάντοτε ἔχουσαν χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ καὶ εὐπρόσδεκτον οὖσαν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἐντρύφα ἐν αὐτῇ. πᾶς γὰρ ἱλαρὸς ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὰ ἐργάζεται καὶ ἀγαθὰ φρονεῖ καὶ καταφρονεῖ τῆς λύπης. ὁ δὲ λυπηρὸς ἀνὴρ πάντοτε πονηρεύεται: πρῶτον μὲν πονηρεύεται, ὅτι λυπεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ δοθὲν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἱλαρόν: δεύτερον δὲ λυπῶν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἀνομίαν ἐργάζεται, μὴ ἐντυγχάνων μηδὲ ἐξομολογούμενος τῷ κυρίῳ. Πάντοτε γὰρ λυπηροῦ ἀνδρὸς ἡ ἔντευξις οὐκ ἔχει δύναμιν τοῦ ἀναβῆναι ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ. Διατί, φημί, οὐκ ἀναβαίνει ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον ἡ ἔντευξις τοῦ λυπουμένου; Ὅτι, φησίν, ἡ λύπη ἐγκάθηται εἰς τὴν καρδίαν αὐτοῦ. μεμιγμένη οὖν ἡ λύπη μετὰ τῆς ἐντεύξεως οὐκ ἀφίησι τὴν ἔντευξιν ἀναβῆναι καθαρὰν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον. ὥσπερ γὰρ ὄξος καὶ οἶνος μεμιγμένα ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ τὴν αὐτὴν ἡδονὴν οὐκ ἔχουσιν, οὕτω καὶ ἡ λύπη μεμιγμένη μετὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος τὴν αὐτὴν ἔντευξιν οὐκ ἔχει. καθάρισον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς λύπης τῆς πονηρᾶς ταύτης, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ: καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ, ὅσοι ἂν ἀποβάλωσιν ἀφ̓ ἑαυτῶν τὴν λύπην καὶ ἐνδύσωνται πᾶσαν ἱλαρότητα.
pass_a_gloss: Take away from yourself, he says, sorrow: for it is also a sister of double-mindedness and of bitterness. How, I say, Lord, is it a sister of these? For it seems to me that bitterness is one thing and double-mindedness is another thing and sorrow is another thing. You are foolish, he says, a person, and do not understand that sorrow is the most wicked and most terrible of all spirits to the servants of God and destroys the person in every way and drives out the Holy Spirit and again saves? I, he says, Lord, am foolish and do not understand these parables. For how can it drive out and again save, I do not understand. Listen, he says: those who have never inquired about truth nor sought about divinity, but believed only, and were occupied with businesses and wealth and pagan friendships and many other businesses of this age: as many as cling to these things do not understand the parables of divinity: they are darkened by these actions and destroyed and become hardened. Just as the good vineyards, when they experience neglect, become hardened by thorns and various weeds, so also people who have believed and fallen into these many actions, which were mentioned before, are deceived from their own mind, and they do not understand anything at all about righteousness, but also when they hear about divinity and truth, their mind is occupied with their own action, and they do not understand anything at all. But those who have fear of God and inquire about divinity and truth and have their heart towards the Lord, they quickly understand and comprehend all the things being said to them, because they have the fear of the Lord in themselves: for where the Lord dwells, there is also much understanding. Therefore, cling to the Lord, and you will understand and comprehend all things. Listen, therefore, he says, foolish one, how sorrow drives out the Holy Spirit and again saves: when the double-minded person undertakes some action and fails in it because of his double-mindedness, this sorrow enters into the person and grieves the Holy Spirit and drives it out. Then again, when bitterness clings to the person concerning some matter, and he becomes very bitter, sorrow again enters into the heart of the bitter person, and he is grieved over his action which he did and repents, because he did evil. This sorrow, therefore, seems to have salvation, because the person who did evil repented. Both actions, therefore, grieve the Spirit: double-mindedness, because it did not succeed in its action, and bitterness grieves the Spirit, because it did evil. Both, therefore, are sorrowful to the Holy Spirit, double-mindedness and bitterness. Take away, therefore, sorrow from yourself and do not grieve the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, lest it complain to God and depart from you. For the Spirit of God given to this flesh does not endure sorrow nor distress. Put on, therefore, cheerfulness, which always has grace with God and is acceptable to Him, and be nourished by it. For every cheerful person does good works and thinks good things and despises sorrow. But the sorrowful person always does evil: first, he does evil, because he grieves the Holy Spirit given to the person to be cheerful; second, grieving the Holy Spirit, he does lawlessness, not interceding nor confessing to the Lord. For the intercession of a sorrowful person never has the power to ascend to the altar of God. Why, I say, does the intercession of the sorrowful person not ascend to the altar? Because, he says, sorrow sits in his heart. Sorrow, therefore, mixed with intercession does not allow the intercession to ascend pure to the altar. Just as vinegar and wine mixed together do not have the same pleasure, so also sorrow mixed with the Holy Spirit does not have the same intercession. Cleanse yourself, therefore, from this wicked sorrow, and you will live to God: and all will live to God who throw away sorrow from themselves and put on all cheerfulness.

pass_b_english: He says, "Take sorrow away from yourself, for it is also a sister of double-mindedness and bitterness." I ask, "Lord, how can it be a sister of these? It seems to me that bitterness, double-mindedness, and sorrow are each completely different things." He answers, "You are a foolish person who fails to understand. Sorrow is the most wicked and most terrible of all spirits toward God's servants. It corrupts a person in every way, drives out the Holy Spirit, and yet also saves." I reply, "Lord, I am foolish and do not understand these parables. How can it both drive out and save? I cannot grasp it."

He says, "Listen. People who have never investigated the truth nor sought God, but merely believed, and who entangle themselves in business, wealth, pagan friendships, and the many other affairs of this age --- all who cling to these things cannot understand the parables of God. Their own actions darken them, corrupt them, and harden them. Good vineyards, when neglected, become hardened with thorns and weeds of every kind. In the same way, people who have believed yet fall into these many affairs I just mentioned wander from their own minds. They understand nothing at all about righteousness. Even when they hear about God and truth, their minds remain occupied with their own pursuits, so they understand nothing."

"But those who fear God, investigate Him and the truth, and set their hearts toward the Lord --- they quickly understand and grasp everything said to them, because they carry the fear of the Lord within themselves. Where the Lord dwells, great understanding also dwells. So cling to the Lord, and you will understand and grasp all things."

"Now listen, foolish one, to how sorrow drives out the Holy Spirit and yet also saves. When a double-minded person undertakes some action and fails because of his double-mindedness, that sorrow enters him, grieves the Holy Spirit, and drives it out. Then again, when bitterness fastens onto a person over some matter and he becomes deeply bitter, sorrow once more enters the heart of that bitter person. He grieves over the evil he did and repents. This sorrow appears to bring salvation, because the evildoer repented. Yet both actions grieve the Spirit: double-mindedness, because it failed to accomplish its aim; bitterness, because it did evil. Both double-mindedness and bitterness are grievous to the Holy Spirit."

"Therefore, take sorrow away from yourself. Do not grieve the Holy Spirit who lives in you, or He may complain to God and leave you. The Spirit of God given to this flesh cannot endure sorrow or distress. So put on cheerfulness, which always finds grace with God and is acceptable to Him, and live in it. Every cheerful person does good works, thinks good thoughts, and despises sorrow. But a sorrowful person always does evil. First, he grieves the Holy Spirit who was given to make him cheerful. Second, by grieving the Spirit, he commits lawlessness, neither interceding nor confessing to the Lord. The intercession of a sorrowful person never has the power to ascend to God's altar."

"Why, I ask, does the sorrowful person's intercession not ascend to the altar? Because, he says, sorrow sits entrenched in his heart. Sorrow mixed with intercession prevents the prayer from rising pure to the altar. Just as vinegar and wine mixed together lose their proper flavor, so sorrow mixed with the Holy Spirit destroys true intercession. Cleanse yourself from this wicked sorrow, and you will live for God. All who cast off sorrow and clothe themselves in complete cheerfulness will live for God."

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, particularly the distinction between 'double-mindedness' (διψυχία) and 'bitterness' (ὀξυχολία), and the complex mechanism of how sorrow (λύπη) interacts with the Holy Spirit. Pass A is a faithful literal translation, and Pass B is a fluent rendering that preserves all theological nuances and causal relations. No omissions or additions were noted.
